question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch settlements and their geographic locations]
options: Cochin – Northern Malabar Coast near Goa
wrong_fact: Cochin (Kochi) is located in southern Kerala on the Malabar Coast, far south of Goa, NOT near Goa on the northern Malabar Coast.
explanation: Cochin (modern Kochi) is in Kerala, in the southern part of India's western coast. It is significantly south of Goa. The Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663. Batavia on Java, Masulipatnam on the Coromandel Coast, and Pulicat (north of Madras) are all correctly located.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch victories over Portuguese and location of the battle/capture]
options: Capture of Malacca from Portuguese – Strait of Malacca, 1641
Battle of Colombo – Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Dutch capture 1656
Capture of Cochin – Kerala, Malabar Coast, 1663
Battle of Swally – Arabian Sea near Surat, Dutch defeating Portuguese fleet
wrong_fact: The Battle of Swally (1612) was fought between the ENGLISH East India Company and the Portuguese fleet, NOT the Dutch. The English victory at Swally near Surat significantly undermined Portuguese prestige in India.
explanation: The Battle of Swally (November 1612) took place near Surat in the Arabian Sea and resulted in an English naval victory over the Portuguese — it was an English achievement, not Dutch. The Dutch separately captured Malacca in 1641, Colombo in 1656, and Cochin in 1663 from the Portuguese.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch control of spice-producing islands and the commodity]
options: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) – Black Pepper as the primary Dutch monopoly product
wrong_fact: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) under Dutch control was prized primarily for CINNAMON, not Black Pepper. Black Pepper was sourced mainly from the Malabar Coast of India and parts of Sumatra.
explanation: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) was captured by the Dutch from the Portuguese between 1638–1658, and the island was valued primarily for its cinnamon, which the Dutch monopolized. Banda Islands produced nutmeg and mace; Ternate, Tidore, and Amboyna were famous for cloves — all correctly matched. Black Pepper was the key product of Malabar (India) and Sumatra, not Ceylon.
